On September 17, they brought the unusual reptile to the Cape Wildlife Center in Barnstable, Massachusetts, where veterinarians have been closely monitoring it ever since.

The creature was born with a rare congenital condition known as bicephaly, which occurs “when an embryo goes to split—like it would for twins or something—but doesn’t separate fully,” Zak Mertz, CEO of the New England Wildlife Centers, which includes the Cape Wildlife Center, tells Popular Science’s Margherita Bassi. “And because of that, each case might have a slightly different orientation; they might have more or less overlapping anatomy.”

The diminutive hatchling came in weighing just 5.2 grams, or about as much as a nickel. Veterinarians won’t be able to determine its sex until it gets a little older. But in the meantime, the creature is behaving normally—swimming, eating and even showing off its dual disposition.
“The left head has the bigger personality,” Mertz tells the Cape Cod Times’ Heather McCarron.
Robyn Rohm, lead veterinary technician at the Cape Wildlife Center, agrees, adding that the left head was “biting the day he came in.”

Did you know? Bicephalic snake
In 2016, a woman living near Waco, Texas, spotted a baby snake with two heads in her backyard. She donated the two-headed Western rat snake to the Cameron Park Zoo, where it has lived ever since.

Diamondback terrapins make their homes in the brackish waters of salt marshes and estuaries along the northeastern United States and Gulf Coast. These aquatic turtles are named for the distinctive, diamond-shaped concentric rings covering their shells, which help them blend in with their murky surroundings. The turtles are considered mid-size; males have a maximum shell length of about 5.5 inches, while females’ shells can grow to roughly 11 inches long.

In the wild, they eat a mainly carnivorous diet, using their strong mouths to chow down on snails, crabs, mussels, clams, fish, worms and insects. At the wildlife center in Massachusetts, however, the two-headed turtle is fattening up on a “delicious mix” of chopped fish, bloodworms, brine shrimp and vitamin pellets, Rohm tells the Cape Cod Times.

The species’ federal listing status is under review, but the subspecies found in Massachusetts is considered threatened in the state. Threats to the turtles’ survival include sea level rise and storms caused by climate change, coastal development and urbanization, vehicle strikes and accidental entanglement in fishing and crabbing gear.
